Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_01
  Name: Anaphylaxis
  Synonyms:
    - acute systemic allergic reaction
    - anaphylactic reaction
    - anaphylactic shock
  Description: A serious systemic hypersensitivity reaction that is usually rapid in onset and may cause death. Severe anaphylaxis involves life-threatening compromise of the airway, breathing, or circulation, and can occur without typical skin features or circulatory shock.
  Epidemiology: Global incidence is estimated at 50–112 episodes per 100,000 person-years, with a lifetime prevalence of 0.3–5.1%. Pediatric incidence ranges widely, from 1 to 761 per 100,000 person-years. Recurrence rates are 26.5–54% over 1.5–25 years. Mortality remains low: drug-induced anaphylaxis 0.05–0.51 per million people/year, food-induced 0.03–0.32, venom-induced 0.09–0.13.
  Clinical presentation: Acute onset (minutes to several hours) of skin/mucosal involvement (generalized urticaria, pruritus, flushing, angioedema of lips, tongue, uvula) plus at least one of: respiratory compromise (dyspnea, wheeze, stridor, hypoxemia), cardiovascular compromise (hypotension, syncope, collapse), or severe gastrointestinal symptoms (crampy abdominal pain, repetitive vomiting). Alternatively, acute hypotension, bronchospasm, or laryngeal involvement after allergen exposure, even without skin signs. Skin involvement is absent in 10–20% of episodes.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Food-induced anaphylaxis
      Distinguishing features: Commonly presents with severe gastrointestinal symptoms; triggered by ingestion of allergenic foods such as peanuts, tree nuts, milk, egg, seafood.
    - Name: Venom-induced anaphylaxis
      Distinguishing features: Triggered by insect stings (bees, wasps, fire ants); typical systemic reaction with rapid onset.
    - Name: Drug-induced anaphylaxis
      Distinguishing features: Occurs after administration of medications (antibiotics, NSAIDs, biologics, chemotherapeutics, contrast media); may be IgE-mediated or non-IgE-mediated.
    - Name: Idiopathic anaphylaxis
      Distinguishing features: No identifiable trigger; accounts for 6.5-35% of cases; requires evaluation for mast cell disorders (mastocytosis, KIT mutation).
    - Name: Alpha-gal-induced anaphylaxis
      Distinguishing features: Delayed onset (hours after ingestion of mammalian meat); associated with IgE to galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose.
    - Name: Exercise-induced anaphylaxis
      Distinguishing features: Triggered by physical activity, often with cofactors like food ingestion; may involve specific foods (omega-5-gliadin).
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Serum tryptase (acute)
      Purpose: Confirm mast cell activation during an acute episode
      When indicated: During acute anaphylaxis (within 15 min to 3 h, peak at 1–2 h)
      Interpretation: Elevated levels support anaphylaxis; normal levels do not exclude it. A consensus equation (peak MCT > 1.2 × baseline tryptase + 2 ng/L) may be used.
    - Test: Serum tryptase (baseline)
      Purpose: Establish individual baseline and detect underlying mast cell disorders
      When indicated: At least 24 h after resolution of symptoms
      Interpretation: Persistently elevated baseline tryptase suggests mastocytosis or clonal mast cell disease.
    - Test: Clinical history and physical examination
      Purpose: Identify potential triggers, cofactors, and risk factors
      When indicated: After acute episode, during specialist assessment
    - Test: Allergen-specific IgE testing and/or skin prick tests
      Purpose: Confirm sensitization to suspected allergens
      When indicated: During specialist allergy workup
    - Test: KIT D816V mutation analysis
      Purpose: Rule out clonal mast cell disorder
      When indicated: In idiopathic anaphylaxis or when baseline tryptase is elevated
      Interpretation: Detection indicates a clonal mast cell disorder (e.g., mastocytosis).
  Pathology markers:
    - Marker: Serum tryptase (mature β-tryptase)
      Expected result: Elevated (>11.4 mg/L) or significant rise over baseline per consensus equation
      Clinical significance: Indicates mast cell degranulation; supports diagnosis of anaphylaxis.
    - Marker: Baseline serum tryptase
      Expected result: Normal in most individuals; elevated in mastocytosis
      Clinical significance: Elevated baseline increases risk of severe anaphylaxis and suggests need for mast cell workup.
  Genetic molecular:
    - Marker: KIT D816V mutation
      Technique: PCR from peripheral blood or bone marrow
      Clinical significance: Identifies clonal mast cell disorder; indicated in idiopathic anaphylaxis or elevated baseline tryptase.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Observe for at least 6–12 hours after reaction, especially if severe or requiring multiple epinephrine doses. Specialist follow-up for trigger identification and education.
    Recommended tests:
      - Allergen-specific IgE testing
      - Skin prick testing
      - Baseline serum tryptase
      - KIT mutation analysis if indicated
      - Periodic reassessment of comorbidities
    Long term effects:
      - Risk of recurrence
      - Potential for biphasic reactions
      - Psychological impact
      - Need for allergen avoidance or immunotherapy
    Survivorship notes: Patients should carry an epinephrine auto-injector, have a written emergency action plan, wear medical identification, and receive ongoing education on anaphylaxis management.

Pathogenesis of anaphylaxis

Despite expressing common clinical features, the underlying mechanisms of anaphylaxis may vary.32 Nevertheless, some of the activated pathways may be common to different types of anaphylaxis reactions or be present simultaneously (Fig. 2). IgE-mediated anaphylaxis is considered the classic and most frequent mechanism. Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_01
  Name: Anaphylaxis
  Synonyms:
    - acute systemic allergic reaction
    - anaphylactic reaction
    - anaphylactic shock
  Description: A serious systemic hypersensitivity reaction that is usually rapid in onset and may cause death. Severe anaphylaxis involves life-threatening compromise of the airway, breathing, or circulation, and can occur without typical skin features or circulatory shock.
  Epidemiology: Global incidence is estimated at 50–112 episodes per 100,000 person-years, with a lifetime prevalence of 0.3–5.1%. Pediatric incidence ranges widely, from 1 to 761 per 100,000 person-years. Recurrence rates are 26.5–54% over 1.5–25 years. Mortality remains low: drug-induced anaphylaxis 0.05–0.51 per million people/year, food-induced 0.03–0.32, venom-induced 0.09–0.13.
  Clinical presentation: Acute onset (minutes to several hours) of skin/mucosal involvement (generalized urticaria, pruritus, flushing, angioedema of lips, tongue, uvula) plus at least one of: respiratory compromise (dyspnea, wheeze, stridor, hypoxemia), cardiovascular compromise (hypotension, syncope, collapse), or severe gastrointestinal symptoms (crampy abdominal pain, repetitive vomiting). Alternatively, acute hypotension, bronchospasm, or laryngeal involvement after allergen exposure, even without skin signs. Skin involvement is absent in 10–20% of episodes.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Food-induced anaphylaxis
      Distinguishing features: Commonly presents with severe gastrointestinal symptoms; triggered by ingestion of allergenic foods such as peanuts, tree nuts, milk, egg, seafood.
    - Name: Venom-induced anaphylaxis
      Distinguishing features: Triggered by insect stings (bees, wasps, fire ants); typical systemic reaction with rapid onset.
    - Name: Drug-induced anaphylaxis
      Distinguishing features: Occurs after administration of medications (antibiotics, NSAIDs, biologics, chemotherapeutics, contrast media); may be IgE-mediated or non-IgE-mediated.
    - Name: Idiopathic anaphylaxis
      Distinguishing features: No identifiable trigger; accounts for 6.5-35% of cases; requires evaluation for mast cell disorders (mastocytosis, KIT mutation).
    - Name: Alpha-gal-induced anaphylaxis
      Distinguishing features: Delayed onset (hours after ingestion of mammalian meat); associated with IgE to galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose.
    - Name: Exercise-induced anaphylaxis
      Distinguishing features: Triggered by physical activity, often with cofactors like food ingestion; may involve specific foods (omega-5-gliadin).
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Serum tryptase (acute)
      Purpose: Confirm mast cell activation during an acute episode
      When indicated: During acute anaphylaxis (within 15 min to 3 h, peak at 1–2 h)
      Interpretation: Elevated levels support anaphylaxis; normal levels do not exclude it. A consensus equation (peak MCT > 1.2 × baseline tryptase + 2 ng/L) may be used.
    - Test: Serum tryptase (baseline)
      Purpose: Establish individual baseline and detect underlying mast cell disorders
      When indicated: At least 24 h after resolution of symptoms
      Interpretation: Persistently elevated baseline tryptase suggests mastocytosis or clonal mast cell disease.
    - Test: Clinical history and physical examination
      Purpose: Identify potential triggers, cofactors, and risk factors
      When indicated: After acute episode, during specialist assessment
    - Test: Allergen-specific IgE testing and/or skin prick tests
      Purpose: Confirm sensitization to suspected allergens
      When indicated: During specialist allergy workup
    - Test: KIT D816V mutation analysis
      Purpose: Rule out clonal mast cell disorder
      When indicated: In idiopathic anaphylaxis or when baseline tryptase is elevated
      Interpretation: Detection indicates a clonal mast cell disorder (e.g., mastocytosis).
  Pathology markers:
    - Marker: Serum tryptase (mature β-tryptase)
      Expected result: Elevated (>11.4 mg/L) or significant rise over baseline per consensus equation
      Clinical significance: Indicates mast cell degranulation; supports diagnosis of anaphylaxis.
    - Marker: Baseline serum tryptase
      Expected result: Normal in most individuals; elevated in mastocytosis
      Clinical significance: Elevated baseline increases risk of severe anaphylaxis and suggests need for mast cell workup.
  Genetic molecular:
    - Marker: KIT D816V mutation
      Technique: PCR from peripheral blood or bone marrow
      Clinical significance: Identifies clonal mast cell disorder; indicated in idiopathic anaphylaxis or elevated baseline tryptase.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: Observe for at least 6–12 hours after reaction, especially if severe or requiring multiple epinephrine doses. Specialist follow-up for trigger identification and education.
    Recommended tests:
      - Allergen-specific IgE testing
      - Skin prick testing
      - Baseline serum tryptase
      - KIT mutation analysis if indicated
      - Periodic reassessment of comorbidities
    Long term effects:
      - Risk of recurrence
      - Potential for biphasic reactions
      - Psychological impact
      - Need for allergen avoidance or immunotherapy
    Survivorship notes: Patients should carry an epinephrine auto-injector, have a written emergency action plan, wear medical identification, and receive ongoing education on anaphylaxis management.

### Investigations for Hypersensitivity Reactions

Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis based on symptom presentation and the timing of the reaction in relation to the triggering exposure. Several biomarkers for anaphylaxis can be measured, as referenced in Appendix C. During an immediate HR, the measurement of serum tryptase is the easiest and most practical biomarker to collect in Canada, as other options are rarely available. Serum tryptase will increase 30minutes after an immediate HR and remain elevated for several hours before returning to baseline. These results can take time to return and must be compared to baseline tryptase concentrations to determine if activation of mast cells occurred, and therefore, are not helpful during the HR, but can be helpful when later assessed by an allergist.

A summary of investigations for evaluation of contrast media hypersensitivity is provided in Appendix D. Allergists often use

skin prick testing and intradermal testing to investigate possible immediate HRs. As many HRs do not involve IgE-mediated mechanisms, skin prick testing has poor sensitivity. Over 90% of patients who have had an immediate HR will test negative on skin prick testing, and approximately 50% to 90% will be negative on intradermal testing, depending on the severity of the reaction.15,97 Despite this, many guidelines still recommend skin prick testing and intradermal testing to investigate HRs. For example, the EAACI position paper published in 2020 suggests a broad panel of ICM for testing to identify potential triggers. To support this approach, Bansie et al reviewed 19 studies that examined patients with a history of immediate HRs to ICM.98 If a patient tested positive for an offending agent on skin prick testing, an alternate agent that had tested negative was used without reaction in 94% of cases. This paper does note that it was rare for patients who tested positive for an ICM to be summarily challenged to the same ICM; out of 7 patients who were re-exposed to a ICM after testing positive on investigations, 6 had a second HR. Similar results were reported with GBCAs, with provocation challenges to alternate GBCA after testing positive to one agent resulted in no adverse events.

It can be difficult to grade the severity of anaphylaxis reactions. During acute anaphylaxis, serum tryptase levels are increased from 15 min to 3 h or even longer, after the onset; levels peak between 1 and 2 h after the onset with 36–40% remaining <11.4 mg/L.113 Commercial assays measure mature b-tryptase released upon mast cell activation and a- and bprotryptase which is secreted constitutively (this reflects mast cell burden rather than anaphylaxis). and instruct them to inject epinephrine rapidly, via the intramuscular route, in the mid-anterolateral thigh, holding the EAI in place for about 3–10 s and then to call for medical assistance.106,107

## ANAPHYLAXIS SEVERITY GRADING

It can be difficult to grade the severity of anaphylaxis reactions. There is no overall consensus on which is the most appropriate system among the several that have been published; this is partly due to some being designed to grade reactions due to a specific trigger eg, anesthetic or venom-related anaphylaxis may rate vomiting as a more concerning symptom, in contrast to those used for food-related anaphylaxis. Further differences can be found according to the systems involved or the intensity of symptoms. A recent article has compared the performance of 23 different systems, highlighting the differences among these (although their validation is still lacking).109 One of these, is the modification of the WAO grading system originally designed to classify systemic reactions due to allergen immunotherapy, but which has been adapted for use with systemic reactions of any cause (Table 7).110 In this classification, only some grade 3 or grades 4–5 would be consistent with the definition of anaphylaxis, while grades 1–2 constitute non-anaphylaxis. Some additional symptoms, such as drooling or neurological symptoms, may be applicable in the pediatric setting.111 The potential for the severity of reactions to change must be recognized. ## DIAGNOSTIC TESTS IN ACUTE ANAPHYLAXIS

During acute anaphylaxis, serum tryptase levels are increased from 15 min to 3 h or even longer, after the onset; levels peak between 1 and 2 h after the onset with 36–40% remaining <11.4 mg/L.113 Commercial assays measure mature b-tryptase released upon mast cell activation and a- and bprotryptase which is secreted constitutively (this reflects mast cell burden rather than anaphylaxis). Although elevated levels support a diagnosis of anaphylaxis, normal levels do not exclude anaphylaxis having occurred (eg, children with food induced anaphylaxis).114 It is recommended to evaluate baseline serum tryptase at least 24 h after resolution of anaphylaxis symptoms, even

when tryptase concentration during episode remains within normal range. In 2010 a consensus equation (peak MCT should be > 1.2x baseline tryptase þ 2 ng/L) was proposed to diagnose acute mast cell activation.115 Nevertheless, the consensus equation and the other methods of comparing baseline and peak serum tryptase are unable to detect all anaphylactic reactions.116,117

## LONG-TERM MANAGEMENT OF ANAPHYLAXIS

Tailored individual anaphylaxis management plans should be a part of the longer-term care of patients who have experienced anaphylaxis, even once.118 Where resources are limited, postdischarge management is severely compromised by lack of availability and affordability of EAI or consultation with allergy/immunology specialists.119

Implementing guideline recommendations in routine clinical practice is challenging.120 The WAO Guidelines for the Assessment and Management of Anaphylaxis in health care and community settings is a widely disseminated and used resource (Fig. 5). Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_01
  Condition ref: cond_01
  Setting: first_line
  Patient population: Patients with suspected anaphylaxis, based on acute onset of symptoms involving skin/mucosal tissue plus respiratory compromise, cardiovascular instability, or severe gastrointestinal symptoms; or acute hypotension/bronchospasm/laryngeal involvement after known allergen exposure.
  Decision rules:
    - Immediately remove suspected trigger if possible (e.g., discontinue drug infusion).
    - Assess airway, breathing, circulation, mental status, and skin.
    - Call for emergency medical services simultaneously.
    - Inject epinephrine (adrenaline) intramuscularly into the vastus lateralis (antero-lateral thigh).
    - Position patient: supine unless respiratory distress (then sitting); if pregnant, left lateral semi-recumbent; if unconscious, recovery position.
    - Repeat intramuscular epinephrine every 5-15 minutes if symptoms refractory.
    - If respiratory distress, administer high-flow oxygen (100% non-rebreather mask) and consider nebulized epinephrine for upper airway obstruction or inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonists for bronchoconstriction (not as substitute for epinephrine).
    - If cardiovascular instability, establish IV access with wide-bore cannula, give IV fluid bolus (20 mL/kg crystalloid), and consider IV epinephrine infusion under expert monitoring if refractory.
    - Monitor vital signs, cardiac rhythm, and respiratory status frequently; observe for biphasic reaction (at least 6-12 hours, longer for severe reactions).
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: Intramuscular epinephrine (adrenaline)
      Summary: First-line treatment for anaphylaxis. Administer 0.01 mg/kg body weight (maximum 0.5 mg per dose) into the antero-lateral thigh, repeated every 5-15 minutes as needed to control symptoms.
      Duration cycles: Until symptoms resolve; may require multiple doses.
  Alternative regimens:
    - Name: Intravenous epinephrine (adrenaline) infusion
      Summary: For anaphylaxis refractory to repeated intramuscular epinephrine. Must be administered by experienced personnel with cardiac monitoring, preferably as an infusion via pump. Various low-dose protocols exist (e.g., Brown et al. protocol).
      Conditions for use: Refractory anaphylaxis with ongoing cardiovascular or respiratory compromise despite appropriate intramuscular epinephrine.
    - Name: Nebulized epinephrine (adrenaline)
      Summary: Consider for upper airway obstruction (e.g., laryngeal edema) as an adjunct to intramuscular epinephrine.
      Conditions for use: Signs of upper airway obstruction (stridor). Not a substitute for intramuscular epinephrine.
    - Name: Inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonists (e.g., salbutamol/albuterol)
      Summary: Adjuvant for bronchoconstriction symptoms after epinephrine administration.
      Conditions for use: Persistent bronchospasm despite epinephrine.
    - Name: H1-antihistamines (second-generation oral or first-generation parenteral)
      Summary: May help relieve cutaneous symptoms (e.g., urticaria, pruritus). Limited role; should not delay epinephrine administration. Parenteral first-generation agents (chlorpheniramine, diphenhydramine, clemastine) available; rapid IV administration can cause hypotension. Some guidelines consider them third-line.
      Conditions for use: Symptomatic relief of skin manifestations only, after epinephrine.
    - Name: Glucocorticoids (e.g., intravenous hydrocortisone or methylprednisolone)
      Summary: Historically used to prevent protracted symptoms and biphasic reactions, especially in asthmatic patients. Increasing evidence questions benefit; routine use controversial.
      Conditions for use: Consider in moderate-severe anaphylaxis, particularly with asthma, after epinephrine. Not for acute rescue.
    - Name: Glucagon
      Summary: Parenteral glucagon may be considered in patients with anaphylaxis not optimally responding to epinephrine, especially those on beta-blockers. Evidence limited.
      Conditions for use: Refractory anaphylaxis in patients on beta-blockers.
  Not recommended:
    - Name: Intravenous bolus epinephrine
      Reason: Risk of fatal arrhythmias; intravenous route should not be used for initial treatment and only as infusion under expert monitoring.
    - Name: Antihistamines as first-line therapy
      Reason: Do not replace epinephrine; they have a limited role and may delay life-saving epinephrine administration.
    - Name: Glucocorticoids as sole acute treatment
      Reason: No evidence of benefit in acute anaphylaxis management; routine use is controversial and may be harmful.
  Response assessment:
    - Timepoint: Throughout acute management
      Method: Frequent monitoring of blood pressure, heart rate, perfusion, respiratory status, and mental status.
      Interpretation: Reassess for resolution of symptoms or signs of biphasic reaction. Biphasic reactions may occur within 6-12 hours after initial reaction.
    - Timepoint: After initial treatment and stabilization
      Method: Observation period of at least 6-12 hours, longer for severe reactions or those requiring multiple epinephrine doses.
      Interpretation: Ensure no recurrence before discharge; educate patient on risk of biphasic reaction and indications to return.
  Supportive care:
    - High flow oxygen (preferably 100% via non-rebreather mask) for respiratory distress or patients receiving repeated epinephrine.
    - Intravenous access with wide-bore cannula (14 or 16 gauge in adults).
    - Intravenous crystalloid fluid bolus (20 mL/kg) for cardiovascular instability.
    - Cardiopulmonary resuscitation with continuous cardiac compressions if indicated.
    - Positioning: supine with legs elevated (unless respiratory distress); left lateral semi-recumbent if pregnant; recovery position if unconscious.
  Special considerations: Pregnant patients: position in left lateral semi-recumbent. Patients on beta-blockers: may require glucagon for refractory symptoms. Self-management: patients at risk should carry epinephrine auto-injector and have a written emergency action plan; instruct on when and how to self-administer epinephrine into the antero-lateral thigh.

#### 13 | MANAGEMENT OF EGG ALLERGY IN NURSERIES AND SCHOOLS

Nurseries and schools should have a local policy that covers the management of any food allergy, including egg allergy,117,118 This includes training in allergen avoidance, food labelling regulations30 and knowledge of which foods might contain egg allergens. Training should also include early recognition of symptoms, knowledge of what medication is needed, where it is stored and how it is administered.

Children with an egg allergy should have a tailored care plan in place, with adaptions made to the school/nursery meals to enable the child to eat a similar meal or packed lunch sitting alongside their peers.119 School trips may require a separate risk assessment. Additional consideration should be given to factors, such as food sharing, food contamination and the provision of ‘treat’ foods,

Any food allergy may adversely affect quality of life, resulting in anxiety and depression.120–122 The constant vigilance needed to avoid egg impacts all aspects of the child's life and that of their family.123,124 The patient may experience anxiety in relation to eating a restricted diet, food avoidance and having allergic reactions.125,126 Children with disabilities, communication disorders and hospitalrelated anxiety may find home introduction, with dietetic guidance and support, less stressful. Children can experience post-traumatic stress following severe allergic reactions. This may become a particular problem where egg allergy persists into adolescence.127 Parental coping is critical in the child's risk perception of allergy, anxiety and coping over time.128,129

Psychological help and intervention is effective130–132 in addressing anxiety, phobias and promoting adaptive coping strategies. This can be accessed via paediatric psychology

question: ¿Cómo se define Egg allergy?
gold_answer: An adverse immunologic reaction to egg proteins, primarily ovalbumin (Gal d 2) and ovomucoid (Gal d 1), mediated by specific IgE antibodies. The reaction is typically immediate type-1 hypersensitivity with rapid symptom onset; late-phase and delayed hypersensitivity reactions can also occur, particularly in the context of eczema.

Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_01
  Name: Egg allergy
  Synonyms:
    - Hen's egg allergy
    - IgE-mediated egg allergy
    - Type-1 hypersensitivity to egg
  Description: An adverse immunologic reaction to egg proteins, primarily ovalbumin (Gal d 2) and ovomucoid (Gal d 1), mediated by specific IgE antibodies. The reaction is typically immediate type-1 hypersensitivity with rapid symptom onset; late-phase and delayed hypersensitivity reactions can also occur, particularly in the context of eczema.
  Epidemiology: Prevalence is approximately 2% in children and 0.1% in adults in the United Kingdom. Onset most commonly occurs in infancy, often after the first apparent ingestion; new-onset egg allergy in adults is rare.
  Clinical presentation: Typical presentation is in infancy, with rapid onset (within minutes) of cutaneous symptoms (erythema, urticaria, angioedema) and/or vomiting following egg ingestion. Severe reactions are less common and may involve respiratory symptoms (cough, wheeze, breathing difficulty) or cardiovascular symptoms (pallor, floppiness). Reaction severity is influenced by the amount of egg ingested and the degree of cooking; raw egg white is the most allergenic form. Delayed worsening of eczema may also occur.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Childhood-onset egg allergy
      Distinguishing features: Usually presents in infancy, often with mild to moderate symptoms; high rate of spontaneous resolution by adolescence; commonly associated with other atopic conditions such as eczema and asthma.
    - Name: Adult-onset egg allergy
      Distinguishing features: Rare; may occur as new onset in adulthood after years of tolerance, or as persistence of childhood allergy; tends to be more severe and persistent; can be associated with bird-egg syndrome or occupational sensitization.
    - Name: Occupational egg allergy
      Distinguishing features: Results from inhalation of egg protein aerosols in occupational settings (e.g., baking industry); may develop respiratory symptoms and subsequently react upon ingestion.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Clinical history
      Purpose: To establish a diagnosis of egg allergy based on typical symptoms.
      When indicated: All patients with suspected egg allergy.
      Interpretation: Rapid onset (minutes) of erythema, urticaria, angioedema, and/or vomiting after egg ingestion is highly suggestive. Mild reactions in a clear history are sufficient for diagnosis without further testing.
    - Test: Skin prick test (SPT) with standardized whole egg reagent
      Purpose: To confirm IgE sensitization to egg.
      When indicated: Moderate‑severe reactions, or when the clinical history is unclear.
      Interpretation: A weal size of ≥3 mm in combination with a supportive clinical history is diagnostic in most cases. Higher cut‑offs (e.g., ≥5 mm in children under 2 years) increase specificity. SPT weal size does not predict clinical severity. SPT should not be used for screening in the absence of suspected reaction.
    - Test: Egg‑specific IgE assay (serum)
      Purpose: To detect circulating egg‑specific IgE antibodies.
      When indicated: When SPT is unavailable, or in moderate‑severe cases to support diagnosis.
      Interpretation: No single diagnostic cut‑off value is applicable across all ages; low levels can be found in egg‑tolerant children. Therefore, results must be correlated with clinical history. Egg‑specific IgE should not be measured in asymptomatic individuals as it may lead to unnecessary dietary restriction.
    - Test: Component‑resolved diagnostics (specific IgE to Gal d 1, Gal d 2, Gal d 3, Gal d 5)
      Purpose: To identify sensitization to individual egg allergens, which aids in predicting persistence and tolerance to baked egg.
      When indicated: When assessing likelihood of resolution, especially in older children or adults; may guide decisions on oral food challenge.
      Interpretation: Sensitization to multiple components, particularly Gal d 1 (ovomucoid), suggests persistent allergy. Negative Gal d 1 IgE is associated with a higher chance of tolerating baked egg. Ovalbumin (Gal d 2) IgE is common but less predictive of severity. Gal d 5 indicates egg yolk allergy and possible bird‑egg syndrome.
    - Test: Oral food challenge (OFC)
      Purpose: To definitively confirm or refute the diagnosis, or to prove tolerance has developed.
      When indicated: When clinical history and test results are discordant, or to assess resolution of allergy. Hospital‑based challenges are reserved for high‑risk patients (Box 4).
      Interpretation: A controlled graded ingestion of egg (baked, lightly cooked, or raw) under medical supervision; positive if objective allergic symptoms occur. Baked egg challenges are used to determine if heat‑processed egg is tolerated.
    - Test: Prick‑to‑prick testing with raw egg
      Purpose: To detect sensitization to raw egg proteins.
      When indicated: Not routinely recommended; may be considered in research settings.
      Interpretation: A weal of ≥13 mm has been reported as diagnostic. Does not predict baked egg tolerance and carries a risk of systemic reaction; not standardized.
    - Test: Skin prick test with baked egg slurry
      Purpose: To predict the outcome of a baked egg challenge.
      When indicated: Research setting; not routinely used in clinical practice.
      Interpretation: High negative predictive value reported in one study.
    - Test: Peanut‑specific IgE (co‑testing)
      Purpose: To assess risk of peanut allergy and guide early peanut introduction advice.
      When indicated: Infants with moderate‑severe egg allergy.
      Interpretation: Egg allergy in infancy is associated with increased risk of peanut allergy; early peanut introduction may prevent its development.
  Pathology markers:
    - Marker: Egg white‑specific IgE
      Expected result: Elevated
      Clinical significance: Indicates sensitization to egg white proteins; supports clinical diagnosis when history is positive but not diagnostic in isolation.
    - Marker: Ovalbumin (Gal d 2) specific IgE
      Expected result: Detectable
      Clinical significance: Major heat‑labile egg white allergen; commonly detected in egg‑allergic individuals.
    - Marker: Ovomucoid (Gal d 1) specific IgE
      Expected result: Detectable or elevated
      Clinical significance: Heat‑stable and immunodominant allergen; sensitization is associated with persistent egg allergy, greater severity, and reduced likelihood of baked egg tolerance.
    - Marker: Gal d 3 specific IgE
      Expected result: Detectable
      Clinical significance: Egg white allergen; may contribute to sensitization profile.
    - Marker: Alpha‑livetin (Gal d 5) specific IgE
      Expected result: Detectable
      Clinical significance: Egg yolk allergen; marker for bird‑egg syndrome; indicates cross‑reactivity with bird feather allergens.
    - Marker: Skin prick test weal diameter (to egg white)
      Expected result: ≥3 mm
      Clinical significance: Supports diagnosis of egg allergy when combined with history; larger weals increase specificity but do not correlate with severity.

    - Name: Prognostic indicators for resolution of egg allergy
      Components:
      - Age at tolerance to baked egg
      - Reaction severity (mild/cutaneous only vs respiratory/multisystem)
      - Presence of asthma
      - Severity of eczema
      - Egg‑specific IgE level
      - Sensitization to multiple egg allergen components (especially ovomucoid/Gal d 1)
      - Number of co‑existing food allergies
      - Atopic comorbidities
      Risk groups:
      - Group: Favorable prognosis
      Criteria: Mild or cutaneous‑only initial reactions, no asthma, low egg‑specific IgE, early tolerance of baked egg, absence of ovomucoid or multi‑component sensitization, and no other food allergies or severe eczema.
      Expected outcome: High likelihood of outgrowing allergy; median age of resolution for well‑cooked egg is 67 months and for uncooked egg 127 months; approximately 68% resolve by 16 years.
      - Group: Unfavorable prognosis
      Criteria: History of respiratory or cardiovascular severe reactions, presence of asthma or severe eczema, high egg‑specific IgE, sensitization to multiple components (especially ovomucoid), and multiple food allergies.
      Expected outcome: More likely to have persistent allergy into adolescence or adulthood; delayed achievement of tolerance to well‑cooked egg and uncooked egg.
      Interpretation: These factors guide the timing and setting of egg reintroduction (home vs hospital) and the need for specialist allergy follow‑up. Children with favorable features may attempt home‑based baked egg introduction from 12 months.
  Follow up:
    Schedule: All infants and young children with egg allergy should be periodically assessed for suitability of reintroduction. Adults and older children with persistent egg allergy should be reviewed at intervals to update emergency medication training, repeat specific IgE testing, and consider component testing and oral food challenges to determine if resolution has occurred. Exact frequency is not specified but typically annual or as guided by clinical progress.
    Recommended tests:
      - Interval clinical history (new reactions, dietary adherence, growth)
      - Egg‑specific IgE (and possibly component IgE) to monitor sensitization trends
      - Skin prick testing when appropriate
      - Consideration of oral food challenge to baked egg or cooked egg when prognostic factors are favorable
    Long term effects:
      - Risk of accidental anaphylaxis, including fatalities
      - Dietary restrictions impacting quality of life and social participation
      - Psychosocial burden: anxiety, bullying, family stress
      - Potential for nutritional deficiencies if multiple food allergies
      - In persistent cases, lifelong egg avoidance may be required
    Survivorship notes: Many children outgrow egg allergy; early introduction of baked egg may accelerate tolerance. Adults with persistent allergy should receive ongoing support and education. All patients need an up‑to‑date emergency management plan and ready access to antihistamines and adrenaline auto‑injectors.

Skin prick testing (SPT) has a poor positive predictive value as a screening tool in the absence of a suspected allergic reaction to egg. SPT using commercially available standardized whole egg reagent should only be carried out if there is clinical suspicion of egg allergy. SPT weal size does not correlate with clinical severity. Traditionally, cut-off levels for egg white SPT weal size of ≥3 mm8,20 have been used to support a clinical diagnosis of egg allergy. #### 6 | DIAGNOSIS

Acute clinical signs have usually resolved by the time the patient reaches medical attention. The clinical diagnosis is, therefore, made

by a typical history of erythema, urticaria, angio-oedema and/or vomiting with rapid onset (usually within minutes) after ingestion of egg. Children with a clear history of a mild reaction to egg can be diagnosed and managed in a primary care setting without further testing. Only children with moderate-severe reactions, or where the history remains unclear, require further investigation to confirm and manage egg allergy. 7 | INVESTIGATIONS

- 7.1 | Skin prick test

Skin prick testing (SPT) has a poor positive predictive value as a screening tool in the absence of a suspected allergic reaction to egg. SPT using commercially available standardized whole egg reagent should only be carried out if there is clinical suspicion of egg allergy. SPT weal size does not correlate with clinical severity. Traditionally, cut-off levels for egg white SPT weal size of ≥3 mm8,20 have been used to support a clinical diagnosis of egg allergy. Higher cut-off levels are associated with higher specificity and positive predictive values, e.g., a SPT weal size of 5 mm to egg white is 100% diagnostic in a child under 2 years of age.21 Cut-off values for prick to prick testing with raw egg are reported as ≥13 mm.22 Skin testing with raw egg does not predict tolerance to baked egg in egg-allergic children23. It is not standardized and there is a risk of severe reactions, so is not routinely recommended outside research settings.

#### 6 | DIAGNOSIS

Acute clinical signs have usually resolved by the time the patient reaches medical attention. The clinical diagnosis is, therefore, made

by a typical history of erythema, urticaria, angio-oedema and/or vomiting with rapid onset (usually within minutes) after ingestion of egg. Children with a clear history of a mild reaction to egg can be diagnosed and managed in a primary care setting without further testing. Only children with moderate-severe reactions, or where the history remains unclear, require further investigation to confirm and manage egg allergy. 7 | INVESTIGATIONS

- 7.1 | Skin prick test

Skin prick testing (SPT) has a poor positive predictive value as a screening tool in the absence of a suspected allergic reaction to egg. SPT using commercially available standardized whole egg reagent should only be carried out if there is clinical suspicion of egg allergy. SPT weal size does not correlate with clinical severity. Traditionally, cut-off levels for egg white SPT weal size of ≥3 mm8,20 have been used to support a clinical diagnosis of egg allergy. Higher cut-off levels are associated with higher specificity and positive predictive values, e.g., a SPT weal size of 5 mm to egg white is 100% diagnostic in a child under 2 years of age.21 Cut-off values for prick to prick testing with raw egg are reported as ≥13 mm.22 Skin testing with raw egg does not predict tolerance to baked egg in egg-allergic children23. It is not standardized and there is a risk of severe reactions, so is not routinely recommended outside research settings.

#### 7.3 | Egg component testing

The egg white components are ovomucoid (Gal d 1), ovalbumin (Gal d 2), ovotransferrin (Gal d 3), lysozyme (Gal d 4) and livetin (Gal d 5). Ovomucoid (Gal d 1) is heat stable and immunodominant.2,3 The role of component allergens in predicting tolerance to baked egg white, or resolution of egg allergy in routine clinical practice has yet to be established.24 Persisting egg allergy is associated with a positive Gal d 1, and a level ≥11 kU/L indicates a high risk of reacting to cooked and raw egg.3 Gal d 1 is also a good indicator of whether the child is allergic only to raw egg, or to both cooked and raw egg.26 The acquisition of tolerance to egg is associated with a decrease in IgE to egg white and Gal d 1.27 When using test results to identify children at a high risk of anaphylaxis, although egg white sIgE levels are more sensitive, Gal d 1 has better positive predictive value and specificity.28 The current evidence suggests that egg components are rarely needed for the routine diagnosis and management of egg allergy in children but can be a useful adjunct for the assessment of egg allergy resolution in adults (Box 2).

8 | MANAGEMENT

- 8.1 | Avoidance diets

Eggs served in a recognizable form are relatively easy to avoid. They are used as an ingredient of many manufactured foods; therefore, food labels must be consistently checked. Uncommon sources of egg include quorn, confectionary and egg hidden in a food, usually ‘egg free’, e.g., pizza dough. Extra care needs to be taken with foods sold loose (non-pre-packed) as there may be risk of cross-contamination. Individuals with severe egg allergy will need to completely avoid food sold loose/on buffets. All species of egg (e.g. quail/duck) are given the generic name ‘egg’ on a label. Verbal and written advice on avoidance of egg products should be provided (see Appendices S2 and S3).

#### 6 | DIAGNOSIS

Acute clinical signs have usually resolved by the time the patient reaches medical attention. The clinical diagnosis is, therefore, made

by a typical history of erythema, urticaria, angio-oedema and/or vomiting with rapid onset (usually within minutes) after ingestion of egg. - 7.1 | Skin prick test

Skin prick testing (SPT) has a poor positive predictive value as a screening tool in the absence of a suspected allergic reaction to egg. SPT using commercially available standardized whole egg reagent should only be carried out if there is clinical suspicion of egg allergy. SPT weal size does not correlate with clinical severity. Introduction Ocular allergy (OA) represents a collection of ocular hypersensitivity disorders affecting the eyelid, conjunctiva and cornea. OA includes seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis (SAC and PAC), vernal and atopic keratoconjunctivitis (VKC and AKC) and contact blepharoconjunctivitis (CBC) (1). These clinical subtypes may be diagnosed and managed by ophthalmologists, allergists, pediatricians and rhinologists, with or without experience in managing allergies, considering clinical history and signs and symptoms, aided by in vivo and in vitro tests (1-3). Although several studies suggest a high co-morbidity of conjunctivitis and rhinitis, conjunctival symptoms are often perceived by clinicians as a minor problem and sub-optimally treated. A recent survey revealed that daily treatment of OA has little concordance with current recommendations(4). Topical ocular decongestants and corticosteroids were used in the majority of cases. This was independent of the specific diagnosis of OA subtype and severity. Topical antihistamines and mast cell stabilizers, which

are the first line therapy in most published recommendations, were used less frequently (4). The incorrect management of OA may increase the risk of local and systemic treatmentrelated side effects (4). This systematic review (SR) intends to provide a comprehensive overview of the currently available treatments for OA and of ocular comorbidities and/or complication, and suggest recommendations for their management using best available evidence in published literature.

Introduction Ocular allergy (OA) represents a collection of ocular hypersensitivity disorders affecting the eyelid, conjunctiva and cornea. OA includes seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis (SAC and PAC), vernal and atopic keratoconjunctivitis (VKC and AKC) and contact blepharoconjunctivitis (CBC) (1). These clinical subtypes may be diagnosed and managed by ophthalmologists, allergists, pediatricians and rhinologists, with or without experience in managing allergies, considering clinical history and signs and symptoms, aided by in vivo and in vitro tests (1-3). Although several studies suggest a high co-morbidity of conjunctivitis and rhinitis, conjunctival symptoms are often perceived by clinicians as a minor problem and sub-optimally treated. A recent survey revealed that daily treatment of OA has little concordance with current recommendations(4). Topical ocular decongestants and corticosteroids were used in the majority of cases. This was independent of the specific diagnosis of OA subtype and severity. Topical antihistamines and mast cell stabilizers, which

are the first line therapy in most published recommendations, were used less frequently (4). The incorrect management of OA may increase the risk of local and systemic treatmentrelated side effects (4). This systematic review (SR) intends to provide a comprehensive overview of the currently available treatments for OA and of ocular comorbidities and/or complication, and suggest recommendations for their management using best available evidence in published literature.

Introduction Ocular allergy (OA) represents a collection of ocular hypersensitivity disorders affecting the eyelid, conjunctiva and cornea. OA includes seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis (SAC and PAC), vernal and atopic keratoconjunctivitis (VKC and AKC) and contact blepharoconjunctivitis (CBC) (1). These clinical subtypes may be diagnosed and managed by ophthalmologists, allergists, pediatricians and rhinologists, with or without experience in managing allergies, considering clinical history and signs and symptoms, aided by in vivo and in vitro tests (1-3). Although several studies suggest a high co-morbidity of conjunctivitis and rhinitis, conjunctival symptoms are often perceived by clinicians as a minor problem and sub-optimally treated. A recent survey revealed that daily treatment of OA has little concordance with current recommendations(4). Topical ocular decongestants and corticosteroids were used in the majority of cases. This was independent of the specific diagnosis of OA subtype and severity. Topical antihistamines and mast cell stabilizers, which

are the first line therapy in most published recommendations, were used less frequently (4). The incorrect management of OA may increase the risk of local and systemic treatmentrelated side effects (4). This systematic review (SR) intends to provide a comprehensive overview of the currently available treatments for OA and of ocular comorbidities and/or complication, and suggest recommendations for their management using best available evidence in published literature.

### Should Allergists Routinely Investigate Hypersensitivity Reactions?

For patients with a history of HR to contrast media, the EAACI guidelines10 recommend skin prick and intradermal testing for both the suspected and alternative contrast agents, ideally 2 to 6months post-reaction. Negative results should be followed by a direct provocation challenge. Skin prick testing uses undiluted contrast (300-320mg/mL), while intradermal testing uses a 1:10 dilution. Various challenge protocols exist in the literature; a recent paper indicated a two-step challenge with 5 and 30mL dose separated by 15minutes can successfully identify patients potentially having an IgE-mediated reaction to contrast media.105 As outlined above, the evidence supporting various testing protocols are weak and unclear. Accurate positive predictive value assessments are difficult due to the rarity of severe reactions and limited patient reexposure data in patients with positive testing. While useful in rare cases (eg, severe reaction to unknown LOCM, or multiple contrast reactions), we do not recommend routine skin or intradermal testing over contrast switching due to weak supporting evidence and limited resources, though allergists with established protocols may still choose to use them.

An exhaustive ocular examination to assess abnormalities of the conjunctiva, cornea, and tear film, together with collection of the patient’s clinical history should always be the first steps. Allergen-specific IgE response should be ascertained: the skin prick test (SPT), along with in vitro specific IgE measurement, is still considered the gold standard for this, although if the relationship between allergen exposure and ocular signs and symptoms is not clear, a conjunctival allergen provocation test may also be performed [1, 17]. ### Over‑the‑counter Medications

One important problem is that patients with ocular allergic disease often self-medicate; they purchase OTC medications and fail to seek help even when those therapies are ineffective [22, 23]. In one study [18], self-treatment measures were the first step taken by 56% of patients diagnosed with AC. Many OTC drugs are topical vasoconstrictors or decongestants that have limited efficacy in OA, as they do not treat the underlying cause of the disease [7]. Conversely, the use and overuse of OTC products may lead to adverse effects such as rebound vasodilation [23]. Furthermore, BAK is a very

common preservative in these solutions – present in over 70% of OTC eye drops – that, as mentioned, has the potential to induce ocular toxicity and exacerbate ocular surface damage [7]. ## Is There Room for Improvement in the Management of AC? AC continues to be an underdiagnosed and undertreated disease [7]. Considering the need for differential diagnosis, a multidisciplinary approach involving allergists, general practitioners, otolaryngologists, and eye care specialists is advisable [1, 17]. It should be borne in mind that in many settings, allergic conjunctivitis patients are often seen in primary care and, when referred to a specialist, those with SAC symptoms are usually referred to the allergist, while patients with PAC are more often referred to the ophthalmologist for differential diagnosis [1]. Therefore, inter-consultation channels or appropriate cross-referral between specialists (allergists and eye care specialists) is advisable, as fluent communication between disciplines would optimize patient care and improve outcomes [1].

For patients with a history of HR to contrast media, the EAACI guidelines10 recommend skin prick and intradermal testing for both the suspected and alternative contrast agents, ideally 2 to 6months post-reaction. Negative results should be followed by a direct provocation challenge. Skin prick testing uses undiluted contrast (300-320mg/mL), while intradermal testing uses a 1:10 dilution. One important problem is that patients with ocular allergic disease often self-medicate; they purchase OTC medications and fail to seek help even when those therapies are ineffective [22, 23]. Conversely, the use and overuse of OTC products may lead to adverse effects such as rebound vasodilation [23]. Furthermore, BAK is a very

common preservative in these solutions – present in over 70% of OTC eye drops – that, as mentioned, has the potential to induce ocular toxicity and exacerbate ocular surface damage [7]. ## Is There Room for Improvement in the Management of AC? AC continues to be an underdiagnosed and undertreated disease [7]. It should be borne in mind that in many settings, allergic conjunctivitis patients are often seen in primary care and, when referred to a specialist, those with SAC symptoms are usually referred to the allergist, while patients with PAC are more often referred to the ophthalmologist for differential diagnosis [1].

Main conclusion: The management of seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis should prioritize topical therapies that effectively control signs and symptoms while minimizing iatrogenic damage to the ocular surface, as many commercial formulations contain preservatives like benzalkonium chloride that can disrupt the tear film and exacerbate dry eye disease.

Narrative summary: This review updates the topical management of seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis (SAC/PAC), the most common forms of ocular allergy, emphasizing the importance of tear film integrity and the potential harm from ophthalmic solution additives. SAC and PAC are IgE-mediated, often underdiagnosed, and frequently comorbid with allergic rhinitis and dry eye disease. First-line pharmacological therapy includes topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, and dual-action agents, with recent additions like bilastine 0.6 mg/ml (preservative-free, once daily, co-formulated with hyaluronic acid) and cetirizine 2.4 mg/ml. However, many older products contain benzalkonium chloride (BAK), a preservative that disrupts the epithelial barrier and may promote dry eye. The review tabulates approved multi-dose formulations, detailing their excipients, dosing, and preservative content. For instance, levocabastine, emedastine, and several dual-action agents contain BAK at varying concentrations, while preservative-free single-dose options exist for ketotifen, olopatadine, and azelastine. Topical vasoconstrictors and NSAIDs are discouraged due to limited efficacy and adverse effects, and corticosteroids are reserved for severe cases under ophthalmological supervision. Allergen immunotherapy remains an option when avoidance and pharmacotherapy fail. In summary, clinicians should select topical agents not only for their antiallergic efficacy but also for their formulation’s impact on the ocular surface, preferentially using preservative-free or low-toxicity preparations to optimize long-term safety and tolerability.

Clinical background: Ocular allergy represents a set of often underappreciated immune-mediated inflammatory conditions affecting the anterior eye surface, encompassing various clinical presentations in both children and adults. Allergic conjunctivitis is the most common form and is sub-classified into seasonal allergic conjunctivitis and perennial allergic conjunctivitis depending on whether the triggering aeroallergen is seasonal or present year-round; grass pollen is the most frequent sensitizer in seasonal allergic conjunctivitis, whereas dust mites and animal dander predominate in perennial allergic conjunctivitis. The prevalence of ocular allergy has been rising globally for decades, with seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis affecting between 14% and up to 45% of the general population depending on geographic area. Despite this, allergic conjunctivitis remains underdiagnosed and undertreated—only 10% of affected individuals seek medical attention, with most self-managing using over-the-counter products and non-pharmacological remedies. Ocular allergy frequently coexists with other ocular disorders such as infections and dry eye disease, markedly impairs quality of life, and imposes a substantial economic burden. Management encompasses preventive, non-pharmacological, and pharmacological strategies. First-line pharmacotherapy includes topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, and agents with dual activity, while corticosteroids and immunomodulators are reserved for severe keratoconjunctivitis. Because many patients receive topical treatments for prolonged periods, the short- and long-term safety and ocular surface tolerability of these preparations are critical; certain excipients in ophthalmic solutions can disrupt the epithelial barrier and tear film, potentially leading to dry eye or exacerbation of allergic conjunctivitis. Clinical background: Ocular allergy represents a set of often underappreciated immune-mediated inflammatory conditions affecting the anterior eye surface, encompassing various clinical presentations in both children and adults. Allergic conjunctivitis is the most common form and is sub-classified into seasonal allergic conjunctivitis and perennial allergic conjunctivitis depending on whether the triggering aeroallergen is seasonal or present year-round; grass pollen is the most frequent sensitizer in seasonal allergic conjunctivitis, whereas dust mites and animal dander predominate in perennial allergic conjunctivitis. The prevalence of ocular allergy has been rising globally for decades, with seasonal and perennial allergic conjunctivitis affecting between 14% and up to 45% of the general population depending on geographic area. Despite this, allergic conjunctivitis remains underdiagnosed and undertreated—only 10% of affected individuals seek medical attention, with most self-managing using over-the-counter products and non-pharmacological remedies. Ocular allergy frequently coexists with other ocular disorders such as infections and dry eye disease, markedly impairs quality of life, and imposes a substantial economic burden. Management encompasses preventive, non-pharmacological, and pharmacological strategies. First-line pharmacotherapy includes topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers, and agents with dual activity, while corticosteroids and immunomodulators are reserved for severe keratoconjunctivitis. Because many patients receive topical treatments for prolonged periods, the short- and long-term safety and ocular surface tolerability of these preparations are critical; certain excipients in ophthalmic solutions can disrupt the epithelial barrier and tear film, potentially leading to dry eye or exacerbation of allergic conjunctivitis. The review aims to collate current evidence on these therapeutic options.

Allergen immunotherapy remains an option when avoidance and pharmacotherapy fail. ## Update on Topical Pharmacological Treatment

The recommended management approach for acute and chronic forms of OA starts with allergen identification, followed by non-pharmacological treatments (allergen avoidance and hygiene measures), progressing finally to pharmacological treatment [1]. Etiological treatment with various forms of immunotherapy can be offered under the guidance of specialists [1, 19]; when specific sensitization is the main cause of ocular allergy, allergen immunotherapy should be considered, as it has shown to be effective in reducing total and individual ocular symptoms of SAC and PAC [1, 17, 19]. The aim of pharmacological treatment in OA is to provide control and relief of signs and symptoms [1]. According to guidelines and consensus documents, topical antihistamines, mast cell stabilizers or double-action drugs should be the first line of treatment for the management of SAC and PAC [1, 4, 17, 19]. Several studies have focused on the safety differences between these different topical treatment groups in terms of the potential damage on ocular surface or their role in the development of conditions such as DED [9, 20–23]. Summaries of the characteristics of approved products are listed in Tables 1 and 2. When symptoms of allergic rhinitis are present, treatment options usually include systemic antihistamines and intranasal corticosteroids [1]. In this scenario, the use of second-generation systemic antihistamines, with fewer adverse events and a much better profile in terms of sedation, is recommended [4, 5, 7]. The potential of some systemic antihistamines to worsen the ocular surface due to their anticholinergic effect should be taken into account [10]. Systemic leukotriene receptor antagonists have proved to be useful in the treatment of allergic rhinitis, although less than oral antihistamines [17]; but they have a limited use for the treatment of OA [1, 24]. Topical immunomodulators such

- as calcineurin inhibitors, cyclosporine and tacrolimus, are recommended for chronic diseases of OA (vernal or atopic keratoconjunctivitis) [1, 17].
